frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and uses pipeline and LNG exports to preserve leverage with Europe. Price volatility and European diversification efforts gradually reduce that leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Southern security frontier
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya strains Algeria’s border-security infrastructure. Competition among Russia, Western states, and regional governments complicates Algiers’ non-interventionist posture.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic finance
frictionVectors.details: Angola is seeking greater autonomy through debt restructuring and diversification, but oil revenues and infrastructure financing remain tied to foreign lenders and multinational operators.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is attracting US, European, Chinese, and Gulf interest because of its access to Central African critical-mineral zones. Competing investment terms could limit Luanda’s bargaining power despite the project’s strategic value.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin’s trade and fiscal position remain highly dependent on the Port of Cotonou and cross-border commerce, leaving the country exposed to Nigerian policy shifts and foreign logistics capital.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel militant spillover
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity near Burkina Faso and Niger is increasing pressure on Benin’s northern roads, parks, and border infrastructure. Security partnerships and external financing are becoming more important to protect these assets.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its negotiating position with major diamond partners, but state revenues remain vulnerable to weaker global demand and shifting consumer preferences.

frictionVectors.title: Power and water infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported electricity and stressed water systems constrains industrial sovereignty. New generation and water projects require substantial outside capital and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector external pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing tighter control over gold production and marketing while seeking to reduce foreign influence. Informal mining, smuggling, and insecurity continue to limit effective state capture of revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou’s reliance on Russian-linked security support expands its room to resist Western pressure but creates new dependency risks. Sanctions exposure and strained relations with regional neighbors complicate infrastructure and investment access.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-mineral prospects attract foreign traders and investors, while weak regulation limits Burundi's ability to capture value and enforce transparent contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Instability in eastern DRC and shifting relations with Rwanda continue to pressure Burundi's security posture and transport links.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, airport, and maritime-security projects strengthen Cabo Verde's connectivity but create dependence on external capital and strategic partners.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago relies heavily on imported fuel, desalination, and development finance, leaving resource security exposed to shipping disruptions and climate stress.

highlights: Oil and gas control remains centralized

frictionVectors.title: Resource-contract opacity
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon, mining, and timber concessions remain vulnerable to opaque state-linked arrangements, limiting public revenue and local control over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cameroon is the main outlet for landlocked neighbors, making ports, pipelines, and road corridors targets for foreign financing competition and regional insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and diamond capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign security actors and trading networks benefit from weak oversight around artisanal mining, reducing state revenue and weakening local control over mineral supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bangui's reliance on Russian-linked forces for regime protection limits strategic autonomy and complicates relations with France, the EU, and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: State finances and export earnings remain concentrated in hydrocarbons, while foreign operators and transit infrastructure retain substantial leverage over production and revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Sudan spillover
frictionVectors.details: Conflict along the Sudanese and Sahelian borders strains Chad's resources and encourages dependence on external military, intelligence, and humanitarian support.

highlights: Gulf and Indian Ocean Partnerships Expand

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and Maritime Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a core sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros's effective control over surrounding waters and migration policy.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and energy projects increasingly depend on Gulf, Indian, and multilateral financing, creating leverage over national development priorities.

highlights: Eastern Security Crisis Erodes State Control

frictionVectors.title: Mining Leverage and Contract Asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-backed investors retain substantial influence over copper, cobalt, and lithium supply chains, while weak oversight limits the state's capture of value.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Backed Armed Groups and Border War
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups continues to undermine Kinshasa's territorial authority and threatens access to mineral-producing regions and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to state revenue and export earnings, leaving national resource control exposed to price cycles, offshore operators, and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and financing provide strategic assets but can constrain fiscal policy and increase external influence over transport and resource corridors.

highlights: Abidjan Emerges as Regional Logistics Hub

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: French, Gulf, Chinese, and other international investors are expanding roles in ports, energy, and transport, supporting growth while creating long-term leverage over critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Supply-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire controls major production but captures a smaller share of downstream value, leaving farmer incomes and national revenue exposed to global processors and commodity prices.

highlights: Ports Remain Central to Regional Trade

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Presence
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and security but constrain Djibouti's room for maneuver and intensify great-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: China-linked port and logistics investments underpin the economy, while debt obligations and competition with neighboring corridors create significant external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Strategic Asset Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy financing needs and IMF-linked reforms increase dependence on Gulf and international capital. Large investments in ports, logistics, and real estate raise concerns over long-term control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, keeping Nile flows and regional water governance at the center of Egypt's security planning.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and limited economic diversification leave the state dependent on foreign operators, liquefied natural gas infrastructure, and volatile energy revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Resource Competition
frictionVectors.details: Offshore fields and maritime boundaries in the Gulf of Guinea remain exposed to overlapping regional interests and external commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's strategic coastline attracts competing regional and global security interests, while instability around the Red Sea increases pressure on its ports and sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide foreign exchange but give external firms significant influence over extraction, logistics, and revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: External Market Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, customs revenue, electricity, and transport links are heavily tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Investment and Governance Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The kingdom seeks foreign investment and infrastructure finance while facing scrutiny over political governance, labor conditions, and the distribution of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and Port Access
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over its energy platform, but unresolved Nile tensions with Egypt and Sudan remain a major strategic liability. Dependence on neighboring corridors and negotiations over Red Sea access adds further pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and large transport, power, and telecommunications projects require external financing, creating exposure to creditor and investor conditions despite expanding state capacity.

highlights: Military transition tightens control over strategic assets
Oil and manganese remain exposed to foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Mining and oil contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transition authorities are seeking greater state participation and domestic processing, creating friction with established French, Chinese, and other foreign operators. Capacity constraints could limit how much sovereignty is converted into revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-financed ports, railways, and export corridors remain essential to manganese and timber flows. Control of logistics therefore remains as important as formal ownership of resources.

highlights: Senegal remains the central strategic partner
Fishing and transport sovereignty remain vulnerable

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked transport dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for overland connectivity, energy links, and regional market access. This improves resilience but constrains independent bargaining over infrastructure and trade policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Limited maritime enforcement leaves coastal fisheries vulnerable to illegal, underreported, and foreign-linked extraction. The issue directly affects food security, livelihoods, and control of national waters.

highlights: Gold and critical minerals drive a sovereignty debate

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector leakage and illegal mining
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining damages water systems and agricultural land while creating channels for illicit capital and foreign-linked operators. Efforts to formalize the sector are constrained by enforcement gaps and local political interests.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and mineral leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-supported stabilization and creditor negotiations limit short-term fiscal freedom, while foreign investors retain strong positions in gold, bauxite, and emerging critical-mineral projects. Accra is seeking more local value addition but remains capital-dependent.

highlights: Simandou is reshaping Guinea's strategic leverage
Junta-led resource nationalism meets infrastructure dependence

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor politics
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project offers unprecedented revenue potential but depends on foreign consortia, rail infrastructure, and port construction. The state must balance control and local benefit against the financing and technical power of external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite concentration and contract risk
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains highly dependent on foreign-backed bauxite extraction and export logistics. The authorities' drive to revise agreements and require processing could trigger disputes with operators and neighboring transit networks.

highlights: Cashew exports and maritime security remain exposed

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cashew dominates rural export income, but traders and processors based outside the country capture much of the value. Weak storage, finance, and processing capacity leave producers vulnerable to external price and market power.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime governance
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port and coastal waters remain vulnerable to weak administration, smuggling networks, and foreign commercial influence. Limited enforcement reduces the state's ability to secure fisheries and collect reliable resource revenue.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures constrain Nairobi's bargaining power with bilateral lenders and international financial institutions. Major transport and energy projects remain exposed to foreign financing terms and contractor dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Northern Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing commercial and security interests around Lamu Port and the Northern Corridor, where Gulf, Chinese, and regional interests intersect. Instability in neighboring Somalia and South Sudan raises infrastructure-security costs.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but leave Maseru dependent on Pretoria for infrastructure financing, market access, and project implementation. Delays or disputes over the next project phase could reduce fiscal benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Customs Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's manufacturing base remains vulnerable to external trade preferences and shifts in global apparel supply chains. Dependence on South African logistics and regional customs arrangements limits policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations generate export earnings but leave Liberia reliant on foreign capital, rail access, and concession operators. The central sovereignty challenge is converting resource activity into durable domestic revenue, jobs, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled shipping, mining, and port-service networks shape Liberia's export corridors. Weak state capacity limits Monrovia's ability to renegotiate terms or enforce local-content requirements consistently.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Institution Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security centers continue to use oil infrastructure and revenue access as leverage. Foreign energy firms and external patrons retain influence because production, security, and export decisions are not fully consolidated under one authority.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, Bases, and Migration Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Mediterranean ports, airfields, and migration routes attract competing European, Gulf, Turkish, and Russian interests. External security relationships can protect infrastructure while deepening Libya's strategic fragmentation.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects provide exports and infrastructure but expose Madagascar to foreign ownership, commodity-price swings, and imported technical capacity. Fiscal and environmental gains remain vulnerable to weak regulatory enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Corridors and Port Access
frictionVectors.details: Resource projects depend on dedicated roads, power systems, and export terminals, giving concession holders significant leverage over national logistics. Competition among Asian, Gulf, and Western investors is increasing the strategic value of Madagascar's ports.

highlights: IMF-backed debt restructuring and fiscal stabilization
Mining expansion faces governance and infrastructure constraints

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms limit policy autonomy while Malawi remains dependent on external budget support. Foreign-exchange shortages continue to constrain fuel, fertilizer, and industrial imports.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: The government is promoting uranium, rare-earth, and other mineral projects, but weak transport and power infrastructure increase reliance on foreign investors. Contract transparency and local-benefit guarantees remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Junta consolidates resource nationalism and strategic autonomy
Gold sector remains central to state finances and foreign competition

frictionVectors.title: GOLD CONTROL DISPUTES
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking greater state participation and revenue from industrial gold operations, generating tension with multinational operators. Gold remains vital for financing the state but is vulnerable to smuggling and insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western and UN security frameworks has increased reliance on Russian-linked security support. This may protect regime survival while deepening external influence over strategic sites and reducing diplomatic room for maneuver.

highlights: Gas production opens a new sovereign-revenue channel
Nouakchott balances European, Gulf, Chinese, and regional partners

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE GAS REVENUE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project can strengthen fiscal resilience, but revenue-sharing, local-content delivery, and cross-border coordination with Senegal remain sensitive. Delays or weak domestic benefits could generate public pressure.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND LOGISTICS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and prospective green-hydrogen projects depend heavily on foreign capital, export corridors, and port infrastructure. Chinese and European involvement creates opportunities but limits Mauritania's ability to dictate project terms alone.

highlights: Stable institutions protect control over a diversified economy
Maritime strategy is gaining importance in the Indian Ocean

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to manage the political and legal consequences of the Chagos settlement while the Diego Garcia military facility remains strategically important. The issue exposes tensions between territorial sovereignty, great-power security interests, and bilateral diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL ENERGY AND FOOD DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius relies heavily on imported fuel, food, and industrial inputs, leaving it exposed to shipping disruptions and global price shocks. Port modernization and Indian Ocean partnerships are intended to improve resilience but also attract competing external influence.

highlights: Phosphate, renewables, and industrial policy reinforce state leverage
Western Sahara remains central to resource diplomacy

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE LEGITIMACY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control of phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and infrastructure projects in Western Sahara continues to face diplomatic and legal contestation. The territory's status complicates investment risk and relations with Algeria and European partners.

frictionVectors.title: WATER AND ENERGY SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Drought and groundwater depletion threaten agriculture and raise the strategic value of desalination and renewable power. Morocco is reducing fossil-fuel exposure, but major projects still depend on foreign finance, technology, and export markets.

highlights: Cabo Delgado security remains the gateway to LNG recovery
Rovuma gas promises are constrained by foreign capital and fiscal pressure

frictionVectors.title: LNG enclave risk
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led gas projects remain central to Mozambique's growth but depend on sustained security assistance in Cabo Delgado. The state risks capturing limited value while carrying substantial security and infrastructure costs.

frictionVectors.title: Resource corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, railways, and export routes remain vulnerable to external financiers and regional security conditions, limiting sovereign control over commodity logistics.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen accelerate strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Recent petroleum prospects have increased Namibia's leverage but also intensified competition among international operators. Negotiations over fiscal terms, local participation, and environmental safeguards will shape sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and hydrogen finance
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed projects could transform infrastructure and exports, but imported technology and external financing may limit domestic control over value chains.

highlights: Military sovereignty agenda confronts economic isolation
Uranium and oil leverage remain constrained by insecurity

frictionVectors.title: Energy and export chokepoints
frictionVectors.details: The junta has sought greater control over uranium, oil, and strategic partnerships, but pipeline and border access remain exposed to regional tensions and sanctions-related constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security realignment
frictionVectors.details: Reduced Western military involvement and closer ties with non-Western partners increase policy autonomy while leaving Niger more dependent on limited security and infrastructure alternatives.

highlights: Oil reform meets persistent leakage and insecurity

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline theft and production losses
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, vandalism, and insecurity continue to weaken public capture of petroleum wealth. International operators and contractors remain essential to production, limiting Abuja's operational sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and port bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Expanded domestic refining could reduce dependence on imported fuels, but infrastructure gaps, regulatory uncertainty, and foreign exchange pressures continue to expose the sector to external influence.

highlights: Strategic autonomy is high but regionally contested
Mineral and security networks draw sustained scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo mineral corridor
frictionVectors.details: Accusations of support for armed networks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to generate diplomatic and economic pressure. Regional security ties risk overshadowing Rwanda's formal mineral-trading and investment agenda.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and investment leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control over strategic projects, but reliance on external aid, concessional finance, and foreign investment creates pressure over governance and regional policy.

highlights: Aid and maritime partnerships shape policy space

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE HYDROCARBON LICENSING
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in the Gulf of Guinea could improve fiscal autonomy, but limited domestic capital and technical capacity leave São Tomé and Príncipe dependent on foreign operators and partners.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The country relies on external support for maritime surveillance and infrastructure, creating leverage for larger regional and extra-regional powers.

highlights: First gas and oil revenues test sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON REVENUE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers greater fiscal room, but foreign operators, project financing, and revenue-management demands will determine how much value remains under Senegalese control.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND FOREIGN ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing access and declining stocks generate pressure from foreign fleets, coastal communities, and regional partners, challenging long-term food and resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from investment and security cooperation involving India, China, and other partners, but must prevent strategic infrastructure from becoming a channel for external control.

frictionVectors.title: CLIMATE AND FISHERIES PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Sea-level rise, ocean warming, and dependence on tuna revenues constrain the country’s ability to manage its maritime resources independently.

highlights: Mining drives growth but limits bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINING CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining provides exports and employment, yet foreign ownership, tax negotiations, and local-content gaps limit domestic capture of resource value.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: External financing for ports, roads, and energy infrastructure improves connectivity while increasing exposure to creditor conditions and foreign commercial priorities.

highlights: Maritime security is tied to foreign support

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE RESOURCE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, and fisheries prospects are entangled with disputes between federal and regional authorities, leaving licensing and revenue-sharing vulnerable to political fragmentation.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, neighboring countries, and international missions provide essential training, bases, and maritime support, but this assistance can shape national security priorities and strategic access.

highlights: Critical minerals draw competing external bids

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and grid constraints
frictionVectors.details: Persistent weaknesses at Eskom and delays in transmission expansion constrain industrial sovereignty. Private generation is growing, but financing and regulatory dependence remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are seeking supply-chain access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and lithium-related assets. South Africa retains substantial leverage but faces pressure to process more minerals domestically.

highlights: Oil revenues remain the fiscal lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on export routes through Sudan, leaving production and public revenue exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption, and foreign operator leverage. Limited diversification weakens sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Political transition and security fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Delays in implementing the peace framework and recurrent armed tensions constrain state authority. Regional mediation and donor support remain essential to security-sector and institutional stability.

highlights: Ports and gold remain strategic prizes

frictionVectors.title: Externalized war economy
frictionVectors.details: Competing foreign networks provide arms, finance, and political backing to Sudanese factions, intensifying the conflict and weakening civilian control over resources. Gold channels are especially vulnerable to smuggling and external capture.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated logistics corridors are critical for humanitarian access, trade, and military influence. Rival external actors are seeking strategic access while fighting and sanctions raise operational risks.

highlights: Gas and minerals attract major investors

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependency
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam Port and regional rail corridors strengthens Tanzania's position as a gateway for landlocked states. Large foreign-financed projects also create long-term exposure to creditor, contractor, and concession terms.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-localization pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in natural gas, gold, graphite, and critical minerals supports growth but raises demands for domestic processing and stronger revenue capture. Contract renegotiation risks could deter investment if governance becomes unpredictable.

highlights: Lomé remains a pivotal Gulf of Guinea hub

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a key transshipment and commercial gateway for coastal and Sahelian markets, attracting competing foreign logistics and security interests. Dependence on external capital and shipping networks limits full strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in the Sahel place pressure on Togo's northern border and transport corridors. Expanded security cooperation with outside partners may improve protection while increasing dependence on foreign intelligence and equipment.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European funding and trade access remain linked to migration cooperation, giving Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Tunisia seeks investment without surrendering control over border and domestic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and electricity vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on imported energy, particularly through Algeria and external fuel markets, constrains fiscal and strategic autonomy. Delays in renewable and grid investment prolong exposure.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline offers potential export revenue and greater resource leverage, but Western criticism, financing constraints, and environmental disputes continue to threaten timelines and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure dependence on China
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lenders and contractors remain central to major transport and energy projects. Debt-service obligations and opaque contracting can narrow Kampala's room to negotiate.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using copper and cobalt demand to attract investment and push for local processing, but foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and logistics. Competition among Western, Chinese, and Gulf-linked investors increases leverage while raising dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and multilateral financing improve stability but constrain spending and negotiation flexibility. Transport corridors remain vulnerable to external lenders, regional bottlenecks, and power shortages.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum value capture
frictionVectors.details: Harare is promoting domestic processing and restricting some raw-mineral exports, yet foreign investors retain strong control over finance, technology, and market access. Regulatory uncertainty limits the state's ability to convert resource wealth into broad-based gains.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and payment-system isolation
frictionVectors.details: U.S. and other Western sanctions, alongside weak confidence in the local currency, raise transaction costs and push the economy toward alternative external partners. Dependence on opaque financing and commodity-linked deals reduces transparency and bargaining power.
